summary: This RFC defines the Trust Anchor Locator, a small file that tells a Resource Public Key Infrastructure relying party where to fetch a trust anchor certificate and how to verify it. It adds support for listing multiple URIs and obsoletes RFC 6490. It was itself replaced by RFC 8630.

eli5.summary: It is like a note saying where to find the official rulebook and how to check it is the real one. It can now list several places to look in case one is down.

questions: how do i use a tal file
what does a trust anchor do
why multiple uris in a tal
subtitle: A file pointing to the root certificate that verifies IP address ownership

tldr.problem: RPKI relying parties need to retrieve and trust a root certificate for verifying IP address ownership claims, but the certificate itself may change when resource allocations change. Distributing the full certificate each time is burdensome.
tldr.mechanism: A Trust Anchor Locator (TAL) is a small text file containing one or more URIs where the root certificate can be fetched, plus the certificate's public key in Base64 form. The public key does not change, but the certificate at the URI can be updated.
tldr.outcome: Relying parties can keep a simple TAL file and fetch the current root certificate without needing out-of-band distribution each time resources change. RFC 8630 later updated this to clarify handling of multiple URIs.

facts.label: TAL file format
facts.value: Plain text: URI(s) then Base64-encoded public key

facts.label: Certificate requirement
facts.value: Self-signed X.509 CA certificate conforming to RPKI profile

today: RFC 7730 is a Proposed Standard for RPKI trust anchors. It was obsoleted by RFC 8630 in 2019, which clarified handling of multiple URIs and improved operational guidance.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) is a system where holders of IP address ranges can create cryptographically signed statements about how their addresses can be used for routing. These statements must be verified using a trust anchor, a self-signed root certificate that acts as the foundation of trust.

Instead of distributing the trust anchor certificate directly, which would need to be updated every time the certificate's resource extensions change, this RFC defines a Trust Anchor Locator (TAL). A TAL is a simple text file that tells a relying party where to retrieve the trust anchor and how to verify it is authentic.
sections.eli5: RPKI is like a notary system for internet addresses. Instead of sending the notary's certificate each time, you just send a note about where to find it.

sections.title: The Trust Anchor Locator Format
sections.content:
A TAL is a plain text file with two parts: a URI section and a public key section. The URI section contains one or more rsync:// URIs that reference exactly one object—the self-signed root certificate. These URIs are separated by line breaks. The public key section is the certificate's public key in Base64 encoding (following RFC 4648), with optional line breaks to keep lines short.

The key is kept in the TAL because it is stable: it does not change when the certificate is reissued due to resource changes, renewal, or migration to a new certificate. The URI may reference different versions of the certificate over time, but all versions must contain this same public key. This design allows the TAL to remain constant while the certificate itself evolves.
sections.eli5: The TAL is like a note with an address and a fingerprint. The fingerprint never changes, but the person at the address can be updated.

sections.title: Trust Anchor Considerations
sections.content:
The trust anchor is a self-signed X.509 CA certificate conforming to the RPKI certificate profile. Its INR extension (listing Internet Number Resources such as IP addresses and AS numbers) defines which resources the trust anchor entity is authoritative for. The trust anchor's key must be stable and not change except for planned key rollover.

For operational security, the entity issuing the trust anchor should keep its private key offline and delegate signing operations to a subordinate CA certificate. The trust anchor must be published at a stable URI: when the certificate is reissued, the replacement must be accessible at the same location. If multiple URIs are listed in the TAL, the same certificate must be found at each location, ideally on diverse, geographically distributed repository servers.
sections.eli5: The trust anchor is like the notary's license. Its signature and identity never change, but you might check multiple copies of it at different places to make sure one is available.

sections.title: How Relying Parties Use the TAL
sections.content:
A relying party (RP) uses the TAL to bootstrap trust in RPKI. First, it retrieves the certificate from one of the URIs. It then verifies that the retrieved certificate is a valid, self-signed RPKI CA certificate that conforms to RFC 6487. Most importantly, it confirms that the public key in the TAL exactly matches the public key in the certificate.

If the TAL lists multiple URIs, the RP may choose which to fetch from based on local preferences: the order given, randomly, or based on performance metrics like connection speed. If the preferred URI fails or returns a certificate with a mismatched public key, the RP tries the next URI. This provides resilience: if one repository goes down, the RP can fetch from another.
sections.eli5: You get the note, go to one of the addresses on it, check that the person there matches the fingerprint, and if that address is down, try another one.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Compromise of a trust anchor's private key would allow unauthorized parties to masquerade as the trust anchor and make false claims about IP address ownership. This has severe consequences for routing security. Relying parties must have high confidence in the trust anchor entities they configure, or they should establish their own trust anchors with constraints on subordinate certificates.

The TAL does not list what resources the trust anchor covers; the RP must read the certificate's INR extension. This provides operational flexibility but means relying parties must trust that the certificate issuer does not claim resources they do not control. Choosing appropriate trust anchors is critical to the security of RPKI deployments.
sections.eli5: If the notary's signature is faked, all their documents are lies. Choose your trust anchors carefully.
